article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 80% Indica / 20% Sativa
Genetics: Quimby × DJ Short’s Blueberry
Breeder: Second Generation Genetics
THC Content: 18–24%
CBD Content: Generally low
Terpene Profile: myrcene , caryophyllene , limonene
Primary Flavors: Velvety grape, vanilla, berries, sweet fruit
Flowering Time (Indoor): 55–62 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: late September to early October
Indoor Yield: Medium to high
Outdoor Yield: Medium to high
Grow Difficulty: Easy to moderate

Whitaker Blues is a true family project within one of the most influential bloodlines in American cannabis breeding. Developed by JD Short, the son of legendary breeder DJ Short , this Oregon heritage cultivar crosses an old West Coast indica known as Quimby with one of DJ Short’s carefully selected Blueberry males. The result is a short, resin-heavy marijuana plant that turns violet and blue as flowering advances and develops an unusually smooth combination of grape and vanilla in the cured flower.

Its effects follow an equally distinctive progression: a brief period of stimulation appears first, often bringing a brighter mood and a sudden interest in food, before the experience settles into a heavier, sleepy physical calm. DJ Short Seeds classifies Whitaker Blues at roughly 80% indica and 20% sativa in structure and describes it as vigorous, productive, and capable of finishing in about 55–62 days.
Genetics and Lineage

The breeder-confirmed lineage is Quimby × Blueberry. According to DJ Short Seeds, Quimby is an old-school West Coast strain associated with Oregon cannabis culture and characterized by a strong, sleepy indica effect. JD Short crossed that clone with his father’s personally selected Blueberry male, creating Whitaker Blues as one of his earliest major breeding projects. JD later described Whitaker Blues as one of his initial outcrosses using genetics from DJ Short’s celebrated Blue line, and the cultivar helped establish his own reputation before he expanded into Second Generation Genetics.

Quimby’s exact ancestry remains unknown, and JD Short has been unusually clear about that uncertainty. He reported acquiring the clone around 2003–2004 and described it as a short, bushy plant reminiscent of an old Afghan indica rather than assigning it an invented pedigree. The plant was known for enormous resin production , comparatively modest flower yield, strong narcotic effects, and an aroma that could shift from ammonia during bloom toward fruit-candy notes when the flowers were disturbed and cured.

The Blueberry side supplies a much deeper documented heritage. DJ Short’s Blueberry family ultimately draws from Thai, Purple Thai, Oaxaca -associated Mexican, and Afghani cannabis populations selected through many generations. In Whitaker Blues, that material contributes color, fruit, resin, and a gentler euphoric component that softens the heavier Quimby influence. The completed plant nevertheless remains predominantly indica in appearance, staying low and stout rather than producing the taller “stretch indica” architecture seen in some other Blueberry-family crosses.
Effects and Experience

Whitaker Blues produces a classic two-stage experience. The opening is more animated than its 80% indica structure might suggest. A slight mental stimulation can appear quickly, bringing a brighter mood, increased sensory interest, and enough cerebral lift to make music, movies, or conversation more engaging. One of the most consistently documented effects is appetite stimulation; the breeder specifically associates the initial phase with pronounced munchies. This makes the beginning feel less like an immediate knockout and more like a brief window of cheerful, relaxed activity.

That window gradually closes as the Quimby side gains influence. Physical heaviness becomes more noticeable, movement feels less necessary, and the high develops into a sedate, comfortable state. JD Short’s description of Quimby itself emphasizes a powerful sleepy and narcotic effect, and Whitaker Blues retains much of that character while adding a slightly more enjoyable cerebral lead-in from Blueberry. For many consumers, the progression makes this a better late-afternoon or evening weed strain than a morning cultivar.

Current Second Generation Genetics descriptions place THC around 18–24%, but that range should be considered potential rather than a guarantee for every seed-grown plant. Phenotype, light intensity, plant health, maturity at harvest, curing, and laboratory methodology can all affect cannabinoid measurements. Larger servings may produce substantial drowsiness and mental fog, particularly for consumers with lower tolerance.
Medical Benefits

The strong appetite stimulation and sedating finish have made Whitaker Blues appealing to some medical cannabis consumers. Marijuana with this type of profile may be preferred during periods when stress, muscular tension, reduced appetite, or difficulty winding down interfere with comfort. The initial cerebral lift may help the experience feel less emotionally flat than a very heavy pure indica, while the later phase increasingly favors rest.

Its relaxing character can also make the strain more practical during the evening for consumers who do not need to remain highly active. Quimby’s historical reputation for sleepy, body-centered effects carries strongly into the hybrid, while Blueberry adds a softer euphoric quality that may make the transition into sedation more gradual.

Whitaker Blues itself has not been demonstrated in controlled clinical trials to treat insomnia, chronic pain, appetite disorders, anxiety, or another medical condition. Cannabis responses vary considerably, and THC-rich weed can cause dizziness, dry mouth, impaired coordination, anxiety, or excessive sedation. Medical consumers should rely on testing from the specific product and appropriate professional guidance rather than assuming every Whitaker Blues plant has identical therapeutic properties.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Velvety grape and vanilla are the defining flavors in the breeder’s description. DJ Short Seeds specifically characterizes mature flowers as pungent and sweet, with grape dominating and a light vanilla quality underneath. That combination gives Whitaker Blues a richer and softer profile than many classic Afghani-style indicas. The fruit is dark and rounded rather than sharply citrus-driven, bringing to mind grape skin, berry preserves, and ripe purple fruit.

Quimby adds another aromatic dimension. JD Short described the mother as producing fruit-candy qualities reminiscent of brightly flavored hard candy once its terpenes were released, despite developing a far more aggressive ammonia-like odor during flowering. Blueberry contributes additional berry sweetness, giving the final cross enough fruit depth that individual phenotypes may lean toward grape, mixed berries, vanilla, or darker earthy sweetness.

There is no official standardized terpene analysis for the strain. Myrcene could plausibly support the ripe fruit and earthy qualities, caryophyllene may contribute subtle spice, limonene can brighten sweet fruit aromas, and linalool may participate in softer floral or lavender-like expressions. Actual terpene dominance needs to be determined through laboratory analysis of the individual harvest rather than inferred solely from flavor.
Growing Information

Whitaker Blues grows short, wide, and productive. The breeder describes it as a stout hybrid with short branches and large, compact flowers heavily coated in resin. That structure makes it particularly convenient for indoor rooms where vertical height is limited. Plants generally focus their energy on dense flowering sites rather than producing excessive stretch, and the naturally broad form responds well to modest canopy management.

Color becomes increasingly noticeable toward maturity. Violet and blue pigmentation can develop throughout the flowers as the plant approaches its 55–62-day finish, creating a visual connection to DJ Short’s larger Blueberry family. Resin coverage is another major strength. Quimby itself was remembered as an extraordinary resin producer, while Blueberry adds strong trichome development of its own. The hybrid consequently produces compact flowers with a thick crystalline surface.

Because the buds become so dense, humidity control deserves attention. Strong airflow through the canopy helps prevent moisture from becoming trapped inside mature flowers. Indoor growers can use topping or gentle low-stress training to spread the short branches, although complicated training is usually unnecessary. The plant’s vigor and relatively compact architecture make it approachable for growers who already understand basic photoperiod cannabis cultivation.

Seedlings deserve slightly more caution than mature plants. Breeder-era cultivation notes warn that young Whitaker Blues plants may be sensitive to high nutrient concentrations and recommend increasing feeding strength gradually rather than beginning aggressively. This is a useful detail for growers accustomed to feeding vigorous indica hybrids heavily from the beginning.

Outdoor cultivation is also possible. Secondary cultivation records commonly place maturity around late September or early October, which gives the cultivar a relatively manageable finish compared with long-flowering sativas. Direct sunlight, generous root space, and a dry finish to the season can increase plant size considerably, though the compact flower density still makes autumn humidity something to watch carefully.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Whitaker Blues?
Whitaker Blues is Quimby × DJ Short’s Blueberry. JD Short used an old-school West Coast Quimby mother and his father’s selected Blueberry male to produce the original cross.
Who bred Whitaker Blues?

Whitaker Blues was developed by JD Short, the son of DJ Short. It was initially associated with DJ Short’s genetics catalog and later became closely linked with JD’s Second Generation Genetics breeding work.
Is Whitaker Blues indica or sativa?
It is strongly indica dominant. DJ Short Seeds describes the plant as approximately 80% indica and 20% sativa in structure, with short branches, compact flowers, and a sedating finish.
What does Whitaker Blues taste like?
Velvety grape and sweet vanilla are the breeder-documented signature flavors. Berry, fruit-candy, mild spice, and earthy notes can also appear depending on phenotype and curing.
How long does Whitaker Blues take to flower?
Indoor flowering takes approximately 55–62 days. The plant develops violet and blue coloration as maturity approaches and is known for producing large, compact, resin-covered flowers.
Final Thoughts on Whitaker Blues

Whitaker Blues is significant because it connects two generations of one of cannabis breeding’s most recognizable families. JD Short took Quimby, an obscure but powerful Oregon-area indica clone, and paired it with one of DJ Short’s selected Blueberry males. The resulting hybrid preserved Quimby’s compact structure, resin production, appetite stimulation, and heavy finish while adding the grape, berry, color, and euphoric qualities associated with Blueberry.

Its garden traits are equally attractive. A 55–62-day flowering cycle, short stature, vigorous growth, dense buds, strong resin production, and violet-blue coloration make the plant practical as well as visually distinctive. The only notable cautions are dense-flower humidity and the tendency of young plants to prefer gradually increasing nutrient strength.

For consumers, Whitaker Blues offers an experience that evolves rather than remaining static: slight stimulation and pronounced appetite arrive first, followed by a deeper, calmer, more sedating state. Combined with its velvety grape-and-vanilla flavor and genuine Oregon breeding history, that progression gives Whitaker Blues an identity far more substantial than simply being another Blueberry descendant.
